title: Why Are New Zealanders Called Kiwis
paragraphs: People from New Zealand are often called "Kiwis." Many people around the world use this nickname, and New Zealanders also use it to describe themselves. But where does the name come from?

The answer starts with a bird. The kiwi is a small bird that cannot fly, and it is only found in New Zealand. For a long time, the kiwi was a symbol of the country. It appeared in company logos and cartoons. From 1886, it was also used on military badges, when a group of soldiers from South Canterbury put the bird on its badge.

However, at first the kiwi was a symbol of the country, not its people. This changed during World War I. Several New Zealand army groups used the kiwi on their badges, and by 1917, New Zealand soldiers were being called "Kiwis."

A brand of boot polish may also have helped. In the early 1900s, an Australian man named William Ramsay started making a boot polish in Melbourne. He named it "Kiwi" because his wife came from New Zealand. During World War I, the British army bought large amounts of this polish for its soldiers, so tins with the word "Kiwi" were seen all over the battlefields in Europe. According to cultural historian Richard Wolfe, this helped connect the bird with New Zealand soldiers.
After World War II, the name slowly came to be used for all New Zealanders, not just soldiers.
Today, most people do not think the nickname is rude. However, some New Zealanders, especially some with Māori heritage, prefer not to use it to describe themselves.
When the word is used for people, it is often written with a capital "K." When it is used for the bird, it is usually written with a small "k."
